title: Chapter 96 – Mother's Roots
html:
[Green Pine Garden – Su Qinghe]

Su Qinghe counts people the way other women count coins.

She stands at the gate of the Green Pine Garden in the gray hour before sunrise, in a padded short robe of old blue cotton, with a bamboo tally-board in her hands, and watches the road. It is the second month of the deep winter, the time of year when the frost makes the ruts ring like iron and the pines on the ridge carry white on every needle. Behind her the Garden is waking up. She can hear the clank of the well bucket, the low voices from the kitchen, the first cough of the forge fire as Old Hu coaxes it from the ash.

In front of her, on the road from the village, six families are walking up the hill.

She counts them as they come. Thirty-one souls. Eight men, nine women, fourteen children, the smallest carried on a back. They bring their bedding in rolled bundles, their pots in baskets, a sick goat on a rope. Their faces are raw with cold and a particular kind of wary hope that she has seen before, in a mirror, a long time ago.

A clan is not made of strong people, she thinks. A clan is made of people who are fed.

"Mistress Su," says the first man, a farmer with a patched cap, bowing so low that the pot on his back clanks. "We are from Green Pine Hill. We have a letter from the village elder. We have heard that the Lin family takes in hands."

"We take in hands that are willing to work," says Qinghe. "And mouths that are willing to be fed. You will be both. Come in. There is porridge."

The farmer stares at her. He has been told, she can see, to expect a hard woman at the gate. Instead there is a small tired one with ink on her fingers and flour on her sleeve.

"Come in," she says again, gently. "Your goat will want water."

* * *

The Garden has grown, and she is not certain it is wise.

She goes over it in her head as she walks the families through the yard, pointing: the new bunks in the old granary, the extra kettle in the east kitchen, the line of low sheds that Old Hu and the guards put up in the autumn when the Court trust was signed. A year ago the clan was thirty-odd mouths and a garden that did not pay. Now it is sixty-four, with the new arrivals, and the beds have steadied at last. Zhong's ledger shows it. Wenjun, the accountant, an old aunt with a hawk's nose and a voice like dry paper, has said in the council that if one more cart of firewood is bought she will resign out of principle.

But sixty-four mouths is sixty-four sets of eyes, and the Garden is not a secret anymore. It has not been a secret since the cradle night.

"Mistress." Wenjun is at her elbow with a slate, tapping it. "I need to know whether the Hill families are tenants or kin."

"Both."

"The council will ask for a vote."

"Then the council will vote." Qinghe takes the slate and looks at the columns. "Kin eat at the long table. Tenants eat in the east kitchen. I would like everyone at the long table by the new moon."

"That is not a question of food."

"No. It is a question of what kind of house we are." She hands the slate back. "I have buried three people from this family, Wenjun. I do not wish to bury any more because someone sat at the wrong table."

The old aunt looks at her sharply. Then she sniffs, which is her version of surrender, and writes something on the slate with the edge of her nail.

* * *

The test is held in the stone hall behind the kitchen, at noon, on a table covered in felt.

It is a small stone disc, flat and black, no larger than a saucer. A root-stone. Qinghe bought it eleven years ago from a peddler who said it was worth forty stones and sold it to her for twelve, and it has been in a box in her bedroom ever since. The hall smells of cold ash and onions. The children of the Hill families stand along the wall in a row, shifting from foot to foot, with their hands clasped in front of them, trying not to look at the disc.

She tests them one by one. The oldest is thirteen, a thin boy with a stammer. He lays his palm on the black stone, and nothing happens, and he looks at his feet. The next is eleven. Nothing. A girl of nine lays her small hand on the disc and shuts her eyes so tightly that her face wrinkles, and the stone gives a faint, grudging flicker of green.

"Wood," Qinghe says, writing it down. "One root. Low. It is enough to start."

The girl opens her eyes. "Is that good?"

"It is not bad." She smiles. "It means you will be able to feel the gardens. Do you like gardens?"

"I like the goat."

"The goat is also a garden, in a way."

Beside her at the table Lin Feng, still wearing the plain gray of an Outer disciple, snorts in a way that might be laughter. He has come back from the Inner Court for the day. He sits very straight, with his arms folded, and the air around him has a faint warmth in it now that was not there a month ago. Foundation Early. She does not mention it. Neither does he. But the children keep stealing glances at the tall quiet man by the wall, and none of them dare ask.

By the end of the hour she has three new wood roots, one fire, one metal, and nine children with nothing at all. She writes it down without a flicker of disappointment. She was that child once. The children with nothing are the ones who cook, and keep the books, and carry the water, and without them no sect in the world would stand for a season.

Nine children with nothing, she thinks. And one of them mine, in a way.

The tally-board fills. She marks a column for each family, a line for each child, a small neat circle beside the ones who will start at the Garden school on the first morning of the new month. Wenjun has already found a free corner for the lessons, and Hu a pile of slates. By nightfall every child will have a pallet, and every pallet a quilt, if the quilts hold out.

* * *

Lin Yue is sitting at the back of the hall.

She has been there since the beginning, a small girl with a thick black braid and ink on her chin, hunched over a slate at a corner table and pretending not to listen. She is not a Hill child. She has lived in the Garden for as long as anyone can remember. She was tested at five, and again at seven, and again at ten, and each time the stone has said the same thing.

Qinghe goes over and sits beside her.

"I do not need to be tested again," says Yue, without looking up.

"No."

"I know what it says."

"I know you do." Qinghe looks at the slate. It is covered in tiny exact drawings of leaves, stems, roots, the veins of a petal, with a note beside each. The child draws better than anyone in the clan. "What is that one?"

"Silverthread. It grows on the north terrace in the wet corner." Yue's voice is thin and fierce. "Aunt Wenjun says it is a weed. It is not. It is a weed to the eye. If you boil it for the right time it quiets the lungs. I tried it on the Hill goat."

"The goat?"

"It had a cough. It does not cough now."

Qinghe puts a hand over her mouth, very briefly. Not a laugh. Something nearer to the opposite.

"Yue," she says, when she can. "You have no root. The stone is quite certain. You will never take a breath in and feel the sky. I will not tell you otherwise."

The child's hand tightens on the brush.

"But there is a thing the stone does not measure. It does not measure patience. It does not measure the eye. It does not measure a girl who sits for six hours counting the veins on a leaf because she thinks no one is watching." Qinghe takes the slate and holds it up. "This is the best herbal drawing I have seen in this Garden. Better than mine. Better than the one in the Sect's own book. You have a craft, Yue. It is not a smaller thing than a root. It is only a quieter one."

The girl stares at her. Her chin trembles, once.

"Jian said that," she whispers. "In the summer. He said there are two kinds of power."

"Did he?"

"He said one kind makes the sky come down. The other makes the sky stay up." Yue wipes her nose on her wrist. "I did not know what he meant."

I do, thinks Su Qinghe. And I did not know that he had said it to you.

She puts an arm round the child, and sits with her until the slate is dry.

* * *

The inspector comes at three, in a sedan chair carried by four porters.

Qinghe sees it from the kitchen window, a stiff-backed thing of lacquered black with a gilded roof and the Court's silver crest on the door. It is not Cheng Yun's chair. Cheng Yun walked uphill, all the way from the village, and apologized to the dog. This one is carried to the very steps of the main house, and the man who gets out of it does not look at the dog.

"Inspector Dai," says Wenyuan, bowing, in the yard. He has been out in the beds all morning and his sleeves are green. "You honor the Garden."

"I come under the trust," says the inspector. He is around fifty, round-faced, and very clean, with a thin mustache and a ring of jade on each thumb. "The Court has resumed its seasonal survey. I will see the registers, the beds, the sheds, the forge. And the new residents." He glances at the Hill families clustered at the kitchen door. "I am told there are many."

"Thirty-one. They came this morning."

"The trust says no new structures."

"They sleep in the granary. No new building has been raised."

"Hm." Dai writes something in a little book. "And the Gate Bearer's family. That is you, I believe, Mistress Su?"

She has come out of the kitchen wiping her hands. She takes in the inspector's face, the smoothness of it, the faint powdery smell. A man who has never in his life been cold.

"I am Jian's mother," she says.

"His standing in the Inner Court is provisional."

"So I am told."

"The Court has an interest." The inspector's smile does not reach his eyes. "A Gate Bearer is a matter of the Sect's security. His family is a matter of the Sect's security also. A family with so many new members and so little oversight is a family that might become... a channel." He lets the word sit. "The Court wishes to be reassured."

Wenyuan has gone still beside her.

"What does the Court wish?" he asks.

"A quarterly inspection, to begin with. All visitors to the Garden recorded. The new families entered in the Sect's roll, under the Court's supervision. An annual tribute, to be raised by one-third, in recognition of the added risk." The inspector turns a page. "And a ward."

"A ward?"

"A child of the household, to be placed in the Sutra Hall's school for the term. Educated at the Sect's expense. A mark of confidence between family and Court." He looks around the yard as if choosing from a shelf. "Someone young. Perhaps the girl with the inked chin."

The air in the yard does not move.

Yue, thinks Qinghe.

She does not turn her head. She is aware, in the way a woman is aware of a pot about to boil over, that the child is standing in the kitchen doorway behind her, that Feng by the well has put down his bucket, that old Hu in the forge has stopped hammering. She is aware of the thirty-one new faces, of the sixty-four mouths. She is aware, with great clarity, that this is what leverage looks like. It does not wear armor. It wears jade rings and writes in a little book.

"Inspector Dai," she says softly.

"Mistress Su?"

"My husband will speak to the tribute. The council will speak to the roll. I will speak to the ward." She smiles. It is the smile she wore for twenty years at a market stall in the town, to men who thought they could cheat a woman with flour on her sleeves. "She is not mine to give. She belongs to the clan, and the clan belongs to no one. If the Court wishes a child for its school, it may ask the child. If she says yes, we will not forbid it. If she says no—"

"The Court is not accustomed to being refused."

"I am not refusing, Inspector. I am telling you who must be asked."

Dai studies her. For the first time he seems to see her. She watches him weigh a thing that is not a woman's face but a clan's ledger, a Gate Bearer's reach, the whole slow downhill pull of a family that has gone from thirty mouths to sixty-four in a year.

"I will convey your answer," he says at last. "To the proper office."

"Which office?"

He smiles his small powdery smile. "The proper one."

* * *

The forge is the one place in the Garden that has never been quiet, and it is quieter now than she has ever heard it.

Old Hu stands at the anvil with his single hand on the tongs and a bar of dull iron glowing in the fire, and does not swing. Around him, in a loose ring on the packed earth, eleven guards stand at ease with practice staves, their breath smoking. Four of them are close to the first stage. Hu has them drilling in the yard behind the forge at dawn, every day, in the cold. Qinghe has watched from the kitchen window and has pretended not to care.

"The inspector is gone," she says, coming in out of the wind.

"I saw the chair." Hu does not turn. His voice is a rasp, ground down by forty years of smoke. "Four porters. A gilded roof. The sort of man who would send a child to school to teach her a lesson."

"He wants Yue."

"I heard." He lays the tongs on the anvil, gently, as if they might break. "I was a one-armed man in a ruined forge when your husband found me. I thought my life was done. I had a grudge and a drink and not a single thing worth making." He looks at her at last. His eyes are red-rimmed and very bright. "I have a forge again, Mistress. I have eleven guards who are almost something. I have a little girl who brings me her drawings and asks how the iron knows when it is ready. I will not see her taken."

"No one will take her."

"No." The old man picks up a hammer. "But if someone tries, I will make them wish they had not."

She does not argue. She stands beside the fire for a long moment, feeling it on her face, and thinks that some of the people in her family are made of the same stuff as the bars he works. Hard to bend. Slow to cool.

"Hu," she says. "How long to arm twenty?"

He does not ask what she means.

"With what steel I have, a season. With what the Court allows, never." He swings. The iron rings. "With what Jian sends, perhaps a month. He has a hand for these things now. I saw the blade he made for Mu."

"I will ask him."

"Do." The hammer comes down again. "Tell him the old man says to keep his head low."

* * *

The stall in the town closes that afternoon.

She walks down to it alone, with a basket on her arm, because she cannot stay in the Garden any longer. The market is nearly empty. A thin snow is blowing along the lane, and the shutters are closed on half the stalls. Her own is at the corner, the one with the faded blue awning and the rack of dried herbs, where she sold roots and tonics for twenty years to pay for rice and bandages. The guild officer is standing in front of it, a fat man in a fur collar, with a list in his hand.

"Mistress Su."

"Elder Gu."

"I am sorry." He does not sound sorry. He sounds uneasy. "The guild has revoked the license. A directive from the Sect. The stall is to be closed while the Gate Bearer is under review. It is not an accusation. It is a precaution."

"Whose directive?"

"The Registry. The Inner Court's office of record." He clears his throat. "They have the power to freeze any trade connected to a disciple under study. It is a rule that has not been used in two generations. They found it."

"The Registry."

"You have not heard of it? A small office. Clerks." Gu lowers his voice, glancing at the empty lane. "They are very polite. Nobody has ever seen one angry. But I would not cross them, Mistress Su. In my father's day a man crossed them over a fee, and the next week his shop was a hole in the ground."

Qinghe looks at her stall. At the faded awning. At the herb rack, with its neat bundles of mint and licorice and gentian, each tied with a thread of red. The little iron scale she bought on her wedding day. The stool.

She was twenty-two when she first stood behind this counter. She had a husband who did not yet believe in himself, a son in her belly she had not told, and a hundred and forty copper coins. Every year of her life since then has stood behind it with her.

"How long?" she asks.

"Until the review. Two years, if the Arbiter's date holds."

She takes down the scale. She takes down the awning, the herb rack, the stool. She folds them one at a time, with great care, and puts them in the basket. When she is done there is a clean square of pale stone on the pavement where the stall stood, and nothing on it at all.

"Thank you, Elder Gu," she says.

"I— Mistress—"

"You were kind to tell me." She hoists the basket onto her arm. "I will remember who was kind."

She climbs the hill again in the dark, with the cord of the basket cutting into her arm, and does not once look back at the square of bare pale stone behind her. Twenty years of her life are in the basket, folded small. It weighs less than the grain she carried as a girl.

* * *

The council meets that night in the long room off the kitchen, seven chairs and a lamp.

Wenyuan sits at the head. Beside him, Qinghe. Across the table Wenjun with her slate and her hawk's face, old Wenshi the cousin with his unhappy cough, Wenqing the quiet one, Hu with soot to the elbow. And at the foot of the table, because he has insisted, Feng. Seven seats. It has not been seven since the summer.

They read the inspector's list aloud, item by item. The quarterly visit. The roll. The tribute. The ward. When it is done nobody speaks.

"We can pay the tribute," says Wenjun at last, flatly. "Barely. If the beds hold and no one falls ill. We can enter the families in the roll. It is no worse than what we already do for the Court. The ward is the matter."

"She will not go," says Qinghe.

"She will not be taken," says Hu.

"There is a third way." Wenyuan's tired voice is very even. "Yue goes of her own will, if she chooses. She is eleven, and she has a mind of her own. She may want to see the Sutra Hall. The library is large. There are herbals there that she will never see in a Garden." He pauses. "She may also wish to stay. We will ask her. We will not tell her."

"And if she goes?" Wenshi coughs into his sleeve. "We send a child into the mouth of the thing. Into a place we cannot watch."

"We send her with her eyes open, and a letter for Elder Ye, and a word to Jian. That is more watching than we have now."

Feng has said nothing. Now he unfolds his arms.

"I will go with her," he says. "To the Inner Court. I am Foundation. I have a pass. I will be there every week."

"You are the first-ranked Outer disciple—"

"I am a man of the family." He looks straight at his mother. "Jian has been guarding us from the front for two years. I would like to guard something from the back."

Qinghe takes a long breath. Under the table her hands are shaking, and she does not let them show.

"Then we vote," she says. "In the old way. Stones."

The bowl goes round. When it comes back it holds seven white.

* * *

Wenyuan is waiting for her at the kitchen door when the council breaks up after midnight, with a lantern in one hand and a folded letter in the other.

She has left the basket by the step, the awning rolled on top of it, and he has seen it. He does not ask. He sets the lantern down and lifts the basket out of the snow, and for a moment they stand in the cold yard with the Hill families' voices coming from the kitchen, the smell of porridge and wood smoke, the fall of snow.

"The Court has written," he says.

"Dai?"

"Not Dai. The seal is plain. Plum-bark paper, no crest." He hands her the letter. "It came by a boy at the gate. He said nothing. It is addressed to you."

She unfolds it. The hand is small and exact. The loops on the d are closed.

Madam,

The Registry notes with satisfaction the Garden's growth. It would be grateful if you would answer one question, which concerns only the record, and which carries no penalty for answering or not.

On the night your son was born in the ninth month of the year of the Black Tiger, who was in the room?

With respect.

There is no signature.

Qinghe reads it twice. She folds it again, along its crease, very slowly. The snow is falling on her shoulders. She can feel it melting through the cloth.

She has never told anyone about that night. Not Wenyuan, not the midwife, not the old aunt who held the lamp. She remembers a cold bright light in the cradle, a breath that was not quite a child's, a stillness in the room like the held breath of the sky. She remembers that she told herself it was the fever.

"Qinghe," says her husband gently. "What is it?"

She looks up at him. At the man she has loved for twenty-eight years, who has never once asked her for a secret.

"They know," she says.

"Know what?"

"I do not know," says Su Qinghe. "That is what frightens me. I do not know what they think they know. Or how they could know it, when no one else was there."
